kurz: How much return overconfidence costs in real portfolios and what additional tax costs frequent trading causes in Germany.

bloecke.md:
Overconfidence is one of the cognitive biases whose price can be read directly from account data. No questionnaire or self-assessment is needed for this. Two figures per portfolio are enough: how often trades are made and what is left at the end.

Brad Barber and Terrance Odean analysed such data. For their 2000 paper, they examined the real accounts of 66,465 US households at a discount broker from the years 1991 to 1996. The average household turned over around 75% of its portfolio value each year, which corresponds to an average holding period of about 16 months. The authors then sorted the households by trading intensity.

bloecke.titel: Net return by trading intensity, US private households 1991-1996
bloecke.unter: Net return falls as trading intensity rises; the most active fifth lagged the market by 6.5 percentage points a year.

bloecke.md:
Comparing returns before and after costs shows where the gap comes from. Before costs, frequent and infrequent traders hardly differed. So the frequent traders did not pick worse shares. But they paid for every transaction, and fees and the [[Spread|spread]] made up the difference.

A year earlier, Odean (1999) had carried out a stricter test. Using 97,483 purchases and sales from 10,000 accounts, he checked whether the securities bought at least performed better than those sold. That was not the case. Over the following twelve months, the purchases lagged the sales by 3.31 percentage points. The swap itself therefore reduced the value of the portfolio before any fee had been deducted. Careful portfolio maintenance through frequent reshuffling thus does not improve selection on average and only causes costs.

bloecke.titel: Effect of 6.5 percentage points over twenty years

bloecke.md: The final values extrapolate the measured returns and are not a forecast. The period 1991-1996 was a pronounced bull market; 17.9% a year is not the norm. What is meaningful, therefore, is the gap between the rows, not the level of the final values.

## Three forms of overconfidence

Overconfidence comprises three distinct forms.

The first is **overestimating your own position in the field**, that is, in comparison with others. In 1981 Svenson asked students with driving licences in the USA about their driving skill compared with the other participants, and 93% placed themselves in the better half. For driving safety, the figure was 88%. In a Swedish sample the effect was weaker, at 69% and 77%, but it persisted. Arithmetically, only 50% can be in the better half in any case.

The second is **overprecision**. Here, estimation intervals are set too narrowly. If someone gives a 90% interval, the outcome falls within it much less often than in nine out of ten cases. This form explains why so much trading happens at all. A trade only comes about if both sides consider their own estimate to be the more accurate one.

bloecke.titel: Share of students surveyed who place themselves in the better half of their group (Svenson 1981)
bloecke.unter: By the definition of the median, it would be 50% in each group (dashed line); the distance between the bars and this line shows the overconfidence.

bloecke.md:
The follow-up study of 2001 with more than 35,000 households shows that self-assessment is reflected directly in trading behaviour. Men turned over their portfolios 45% more often than women. The loss of return caused by trading was 2.65 percentage points a year for men and 1.72 for women. The difference of just under one percentage point arose from the women's lower trading frequency, not from better selection. Among single people, the gap was even larger. Gender serves here only as an easily measurable proxy for self-confidence. Trading frequency determines the loss of return, and it can also be used to estimate the damage in your own case.

The third form is the **illusion of control**. Here, random outcomes are experienced as controllable. In 2003 Fenton-O'Creevy and colleagues studied traders at London investment banks. Traders who most strongly believed they could influence the market were rated significantly worse in analysis and risk management, contributed less to profits and earned less. The illusion of control grows with the tools available. Charts, indicators and one-click orders create a sense of controllability that does not match how prices are formed in the short term.

The savings amount, costs, diversification, timing of tax and holding period are controllable; prices are not. Every hour spent on following prices is missing for the controllable factors. Only these reliably improve the outcome.

## Overconfidence after periods of gains

Overconfidence depends on what has happened so far and rises after gains. In 2001 Gervais and Odean modelled how a trader becomes overconfident by attributing successes to himself and failures to the market. Such successes pile up in phases of rising prices. The DAX gained 20.3% in 2023, 18.8% in 2024 and 23.0% in 2025. In these three years, almost every purchase decision looked right in hindsight. Investors who started during this phase have never been able to measure their skill separately from the direction of the market. The same time series also contains the years 2002 with -43.9% and 2008 with -40.4%.

The statement “trading hardly costs me anything” is often true of fees in 2026 and yet wrong overall. An order fee close to zero lowers the inhibition threshold and thus increases trading frequency, the very variable that causes the damage. Push notifications and the display of daily performance in red and green work in the same direction. Spread and tax are also incurred when the order fee is zero.

## Tax costs in Germany

Since Barber and Odean's measurements, the cost structure has shifted, but the costs have remained. At neobrokers, the order fee has often fallen to one euro or zero. Two items remain. The first is the bid-ask spread, which outside the main trading hours and for smaller stocks is considerably larger than any visible fee rate. The second, and larger, is tax.

Realised price gains on securities are income from capital assets under Section 20(2) EStG (Income Tax Act) and are subject to the special tax rate of 25% (Section 32d(1) EStG). In addition, there is the solidarity surcharge of 5.5% on the tax, making 26.375% in total, or around 27.8% to 28.0% with church tax. The [[Saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)]] of €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG), only covers the first income. For units in equity funds, the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] of 30% under Section 20(1) InvStG (Investment Tax Act) reduces the tax base, so that the effective burden falls to around 18.46%. There is no such relief for individual shares. For tax purposes, the units acquired first are deemed to have been sold first (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG). With top-up purchases and later partial sales, the oldest and therefore usually largest gains are automatically realised. In addition, losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) EStG). This further delays the tax use of losses from bad purchases.

Every realised gain thus triggers tax, and from then on the amount paid permanently stops earning returns. This effect does not depend on selection and occurs even if every single decision was right.

bloecke.erklaerung: If every gain is realised immediately, only the after-tax amount earns returns from the following year onwards. When holding, the tax portion also continues to earn returns, and the tax is only due at the end.
variablen: Tax rate on realised gains: 0.26375 for individual shares, around 0.1846 for equity funds with partial exemption

bloecke.md:
In this illustrative calculation, both portfolios start with €50,000 in individual shares and earn a gross return of 7% a year. Portfolio A remains unchanged and is only sold at the end. Portfolio B is completely turned over once a year, so its gains are realised and taxed every year. In both portfolios, the saver's allowance is assumed to have already been used up by other capital income.

- Portfolio A reaches 50,000 × 1.07^20 = €193,484. From the gain of €143,484, 26.375% tax is deducted, that is €37,844. Net, €155,640 remains.
- After tax, portfolio B grows by only 5.15375% a year (rounded 5.15%). 50,000 × 1.0515375^20 gives €136,605.

The difference is around €19,000, or just over 12% of final wealth. It arises solely from the timing of taxation, without fees, spread or poorer selection. With an equity ETF and partial exemption, the difference falls to around €15,000 but remains. The [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]] is not taken into account here. For accumulating funds, it brings forward a small part of the tax and slightly reduces the advantage of holding.

bloecke.titel: Portfolio value after tax, €50,000 and 7% gross (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: Both curves show what would remain after tax on a sale in the year in question; the gap widens because in portfolio B the tax portion never earns returns.

serien.name: Hold, tax only at the end

bloecke.md:
## A forecast journal as an antidote

Knowing about overconfidence does not eliminate it. What works is a measurement that cannot be distorted by later memory. A forecast journal serves this purpose: a record from which the hit rate and interval width can be counted afterwards.

schritte.titel: Write it down before the order
schritte.text: Note the date, security, price and number of units, plus, in two sentences, the specific statement about the future that justifies the purchase. If this statement cannot be formulated, there is no thesis, and the purchase is based on an impulse.
Instead of “will rise”, note a range, for example “price in 12 months between X and Y, with 90% certainty”. Then double the range, because the original one is very likely too narrow.
Set a specific date, usually twelve months later. Without a deadline, a thesis is held until it happens to fit.
Write down three observations that would refute the thesis. If they occur, sell without reopening the decision.
On the review date, calculate three figures: the share of outcomes within the interval, the hit rate of the directional forecasts and the comparison with the alternative of doing nothing.

bloecke.md:
With twenty forecasts using a 90% interval, about eighteen outcomes should fall within the interval. If only eleven do, that is due to the interval being too narrow, not to an unusual market. This is overprecision expressed in numbers. It can be corrected by deliberately choosing wider intervals.

The second yardstick is almost always forgotten. Every decision should be compared with the alternative of “doing nothing”. In a year like 2024, almost all purchases were in profit. Only the gap to the unchanged portfolio is meaningful.

It is said of André Kostolany that a broker closed his account because he traded too rarely. This is not independently documented. The conflict of interest behind it does exist, however, because a broker who earns from transactions has no interest in long holding periods.

The finding speaks against sales driven by self-confidence, not against sales in general. Rule-based sales are something different from acting out of conviction:

- Rebalancing according to predefined ranges, not according to price levels.
- Using up the saver's allowance, because gains of up to €1,000 a year remain tax-free anyway. If they are never realised, the allowance goes unused.
- Loss offsetting within the pots of Section 20(6) EStG, when there are realised gains to set against the losses.
- A changed investment horizon, for example before a planned property purchase.
- A refuted thesis, demonstrable by the criteria noted in advance and not by the price.

All other sales merely increase trading frequency, whose costs have been measured empirically. The [[Disposition effect|disposition effect]] is a separate matter. It concerns the direction of sales, not their number.

mitnehmen: The damage from overconfidence comes from trading frequency and not from poor selection, because in gross terms frequent and infrequent traders hardly differed, while in net terms 7.1 percentage points a year separated them.
In Odean's data, the shares bought performed 3.31 percentage points worse over twelve months than those sold, so the swap itself cost return even before fees.
In Germany, the brought-forward taxation costs extra, because the 26.375% tax on every realised gain permanently stops earning returns: in the model, around €19,000 over 20 years.
Overconfidence rises after profitable years, because successes are attributed to your own skill and failures to the market.
What works against overconfidence is measurement, with a written forecast including an interval, a fixed review date and a count against the alternative of doing nothing; insight alone is not enough.

begriffe.text: Systematic overestimation of your own skill, your own precision and your own position compared with others. On the stock exchange, it shows up measurably as increased trading frequency.
A form of overconfidence in which estimation intervals are set too narrowly. In practice, a stated 90% interval is right much less often than in nine out of ten cases.
The perception of being able to control random outcomes. It is reinforced by tools such as charts, indicators and real-time portfolio views.
The share of portfolio value that is turned over within a year. A turnover of 75% corresponds to an average holding period of around 16 months.
The match between the stated and the achieved hit rate. You are well calibrated if your 90% statements turn out to be right in about 90% of cases.
